rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says the messengers despaired of their peoples, while their peoples thought the messengers had lied.
rows.anchor: من قومهم، وظن قومهم أن الرسل قد كذبت

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: In a second report, Saʿīd gives the same explanation: messengers despaired of their peoples and the peoples thought them false.
rows.anchor: سألني سيد من ساداتكم عن هذه الآية، فقلت: استيأس الرسل من قومهم

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the messengers despaired of their people believing; the polytheists thought God's promise of victory had failed, then the messengers were rescued.
rows.anchor: استيأس الرسل أن يؤمن قومهم بهم، وظن قومهم المشركون أن الرسل قد كذبوا

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الحارث
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith says messengers despaired of their peoples' faith, while the people thought the messengers had lied about their message.
rows.anchor: وظن القوم أنهم قد كذبوهم فيما جاءوهم به

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the peoples thought their messengers had lied about what they promised.
rows.anchor: ظن قومهم أن رسلهم قد كذبوهم فيما وعدوهم به

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says the messengers despaired of their peoples believing, and the peoples thought them false when events were delayed; he read the verb lightly.
rows.anchor: استيأس الرسل من إيمان قومهم أن يؤمنوا بهم، وظن قومهم حين أبطأ الأمر أنهم قد كذبوا

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr also glosses the messengers' despair as despair of their people's help, while the people thought them false.
rows.anchor: استيأس الرسل من نصر قومهم، وظن قوم الرسل أن الرسل قد كذبوهم

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd says the messengers despaired of being believed, while their peoples thought they had lied.
rows.anchor: أن يصدقوهم، وظن قومهم أن الرسل قد كذبوهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās likewise says the messengers despaired of their peoples believing them and the peoples thought them false.
rows.anchor: أن يصدقهم قومهم، وظن قومهم أن الرسل قد كذبوهم

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says messengers despaired of a response and belief, and the people thought the messengers had lied about the promise.
rows.anchor: استيأسوا من قومهم أن يجيبوهم، ويؤمنوا بهم، وظنوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers the light reading with the peoples as subject of “thought”: context after 12:109 shows the messengers despaired of the doomed peoples' faith.
rows.anchor: فكان ذلك دليلا على أن إياس الرسل كان من إيمان قومهم الذين أهلكوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following phrase about saving whom God wills confirms it was the destroyed peoples who thought the messengers had lied and rejected them.
rows.anchor: إذ الذين أهلكوا هم الذين ظنوا أن الرسل قد كذبتهم، فكذبوهم

rows.speaker: قوم ممن قرأ هذه القراءة
rows.claim: Some who use the light reading instead make the messengers the subject: they despaired of faith and thought the promised victory had failed.
rows.anchor: وقد ذهب قوم ممن قرأ هذه القراءة إلى غير التأويل الذي اخترنا، ووجهوا معناه إلى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: An alternative attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās says the messengers were human, weakened, and despaired.
rows.anchor: كانوا بشرا، ضعفوا ويئسوا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the messengers were human and thought they had been denied; he recites 2:214 about the Messenger and believers asking when God's help will come.
rows.anchor: كانوا بشرا، وتلا ابن عباس

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd gives the cryptic response “that is what you dislike” when asked about the lightly read wording.
rows.anchor: عن مسروق، أن رجلا سأل عبد الله بن مسعود

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd accepts that the messengers thought they had been denied, adding that they were human.
rows.anchor: قلت: كذبوا؟ قال: «نعم، ألم يكونوا بشرا»

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿIkrima reports Ibn ʿAbbās as saying the messengers were human and had thought.
rows.anchor: «كانوا بشرا قد ظنوا» وهذا تأويل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī rejects the interpretation that the messengers doubted God's promise: it conflicts with their prophetic qualities despite their clearer access to God's proofs than their people.
rows.anchor: وخلافه من القول أشبه بصفات الأنبياء والرسل، إن جاز أن يرتابوا بوعد الله إياهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is again reported as saying the messengers were human, weakened, and despaired.
rows.anchor: كانوا بشرا ضعفوا ويئسوا

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha rejects uncertainty about God's promised outcome for the messengers; prolonged trials made them think followers had denied them, and she reads the verb emphatically.
rows.anchor: لم يزل البلاء بالرسل، حتى ظن الأنبياء أن من تبعهم قد كذبوهم

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha says the messengers knew God's promise would come; they thought believing followers denied them after revelation was delayed and hardship intensified.
rows.anchor: ما وعد الله محمدا صلى الله عليه وسلم من شيء إلا وقد علم أنه سيكون حتى مات

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Asked about the wording, ʿĀʾisha says the messengers did not doubt; rather, they thought followers had denied them as revelation lagged and hardship grew.
rows.anchor: إنما هم أتباع الرسل، لما استأخر عنهم الوحي، واشتد عليهم البلاء

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha's emphatic reading means the messengers thought believing followers had denied them and abandoned faith while awaiting rescue.
rows.anchor: وظنت الرسل أن من قد آمن من قومهم قد كذبوهم

rows.speaker: قوم ممن قرأ بالتشديد
rows.claim: Other emphatic-form readers take “thought” as certainty: messengers despaired of their peoples' faith and knew the peoples had denied them.
rows.anchor: وظنت الرسل: بمعنى واستيقنت أنهم قد كذبهم أممهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This alternative explains ظن as knowledge conveyed by report rather than direct sight, citing poetry about knowing two thousand horsemen are armed.
rows.anchor: الظن في هذا بمعنى العلم، من قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda say messengers despaired of their peoples' faith, knew there was no good or belief among them, then received God's help.
rows.anchor: أي استيقنوا أنه لا خير عند قومهم، ولا إيمان، جاءهم نصرنا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda separately glosses the wording as the messengers knowing their people had denied them.
rows.anchor: قال: وعلموا أنهم قد كذبوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī objects that companions did not understand ظن as certainty here and Arabic uses it for reported knowledge, not what is directly witnessed; messengers saw and heard their peoples' denials.
rows.anchor: فأما ما كان من علم أدرك من وجه المشاهدة والمعاينة فإنها لا تستعمل فيه الظن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic form with a ḍamma on kāf was read by most reciters in Medina, Basra, and Syria, though al-Ṭabarī prefers another reading and explanation.
rows.anchor: وبهذه القراءة كانت تقرأ عامة قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام، أعني بتشديد الذال

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī introduces a reading attributed to Mujāhid that differs from all previously named readers and interpretations.
rows.anchor: وروي عن مجاهد في ذلك قول هو خلاف جميع ما ذكرنا من أقوال الماضين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid reads the verb with fatḥa on kāf and light dhāl, unlike the other reciters cited.
rows.anchor: (كذبوا) بفتح الكاف بالتخفيف

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says messengers despaired their people would be punished, while people thought the messengers lied; he connects the scene to unbelievers' boast in 40:83 and punishment in 39:48.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد: " استيأس الرجل أن تعذب قومهم، وظن قومهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī does not permit Mujāhid's reading because recognized regional reciters unanimously read otherwise.
rows.anchor: وهذه القراءة لا أستجيز القراءة بها، لإجماع الحجة من قراء الأمصار على خلافها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If permissible, al-Ṭabarī says the reading could mean messengers despaired of God's punishing their deniers and knew people falsely charged them with lying.
rows.anchor: ولو جازت القراءة بذلك لاحتمل وجها من التأويل، وهو أحسن مما تأوله مجاهد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses rescue as God saving the messengers and whom He wills; obedience brings salvation and disobedience punishment.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس: (فننجي من نشاء) فننجي الرسل ومن نشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says Joseph's story teaches how God raised him from the pit, slavery, and long imprisonment to rule, victory over his brothers, and reunion with his family.
rows.anchor: بعد أن ألقي يوسف في الجب ليهلك، ثم بيع بيع العبيد بالخسيس من الثمن، وبعد الإسار والحبس الطويل، ملكه مصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lesson addresses Quraysh: the God who raised Joseph can remove Muhammad from their midst, make him victorious, and empower him despite hardships.
rows.anchor: للمشركين من قريش من قوم نبيه محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid interprets the lesson as being for Joseph and his brothers.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد، قوله: {لقد كان في قصصهم عبرة لأولي الألباب} [يوسف: 111] قال: «يوسف وإخوته»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers a general lesson for all people of reason: the verse follows a warning to Quraysh, breaks from the Joseph narrative, and says all people of intellect can benefit.
rows.anchor: ومع ذلك أنه خبر عام عن جميع ذوي الألباب، أن قصصهم لهم عبرة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī's heading says the account is not fabricated; Qatāda glosses fabrication as a lie.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة: " {ما كان حديثا يفترى} [يوسف: 111] والفرية: الكذب

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses “fabrication” as a lie.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة: " {ما كان حديثا يفترى} [يوسف: 111] والفرية: الكذب

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī explains that the Qurʾān confirms earlier revealed books; Qatāda says the Furqān confirms earlier scriptures and bears witness to them.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة: " {ولكن تصديق الذي بين يديه} [يونس: 37] والفرقان تصديق الكتب التي قبله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the Furqān confirms earlier scriptures and bears witness to them.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة: " {ولكن تصديق الذي بين يديه} [يونس: 37] والفرقان تصديق الكتب التي قبله، ويشهد عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī reads Subḥāna as declaring God transcendent and absolving Him of partners, spouse, and child attributed by polytheists.
rows.anchor: بعبده وتبرئة له مما يقول فيه المشركون من أن له من خلقه شريكا وأن له صاحبة وولدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Subḥān is a noun used in place of a verbal noun and is accusative in that function; some instead say its accusative reflects its being indefinite.
rows.anchor: اسم وضع موضع المصدر فنصب لوقوعه موقعه بما أغنى عن إعادته

rows.speaker: أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Many interpreters take tasbīḥ as prayer in 37:143, understanding Jonah as one of those who pray.
rows.anchor: فلولا أنه كان من المصلين

rows.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Some interpreters take tasbīḥ as making an exception, citing 68:18 and the reminder in 68:28; this was said to be usage among some Yemenis.
rows.anchor: وزعم أن ذلك لغة لبعض أهل اليمن

rows.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Some understand the prophetic phrase about the face's “subuḥāt” as its light.
rows.anchor: سبحات وجهه: نور وجهه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report through Mūsā ibn Ṭalḥa explains saying Subḥān Allāh as declaring God free of evil.
rows.anchor: عن موسى بن طلحة، عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه سئل عن التسبيح أن يقول الإنسان: سبحان الله، قال: «إنزاه الله عن السوء»

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid glosses Subḥān Allāh as declaring God pure.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد، قوله: سبحان الله: قال: إنكاف لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī defines al-isrāʾ and al-surā as travel by night.
rows.anchor: والإسراء والسرى: سير الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī cites a poetic line using saraytu to illustrate sarā as night travel.
rows.anchor: وليلة ذات دجى سريت … ولم يلتني عن سراها ليت

rows.speaker: حذيفة بن اليمان
rows.claim: Ḥudhayfa recited “from the night” after “his servant,” as did ʿAbd Allāh.
rows.anchor: قرأ حذيفة: (سبحان الذي أسرى بعبده من الليل من المسجد الحرام إلى المسجد الأقصى)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poem is also transmitted with the variant wording “a night of dew” instead of “a night of darkness.”
rows.anchor: ويروى: ذات ندى سريت

rows.speaker: أم هانئ بنت أبي طالب
rows.claim: Umm Hāniʾ says the Prophet told her he prayed ʿishāʾ with them in the valley, went to Jerusalem, and returned to pray dawn with them.
rows.anchor: فلما صلى الصبح وصلينا معه قال: «يا أم هانئ لقد صليت معكم العشاء الآخرة

rows.speaker: أم هانئ بنت أبي طالب
rows.claim: Umm Hāniʾ says the Prophet spent the night journey asleep at her house, sleeping after the night prayer before being woken near dawn.
rows.anchor: عن أم هانئ بنت أبي طالب، في مسرى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، أنها كانت تقول

rows.speaker: أنس عن مالك بن صعصعة عن النبي
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet was at the House between sleep and wakefulness, had his chest washed with Zamzam, rode Buraq to Jerusalem, led the prophets in prayer, then ascended.
rows.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك، عن مالك بن صعصعة، وهو رجل من قومه قال: قال نبي الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري عن النبي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reports the Prophet asleep in the Hijr before Gabriel woke him, led him from the mosque, and brought a white Buraq.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن بن أبي الحسن، قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «بينا أنا نائم

rows.speaker: أنس عن شريك بن أبي نمر
rows.claim: Anas reports three figures came to the sleeping Prophet in the Sacred Mosque; Gabriel opened his chest, purified it and filled it with faith and wisdom, then took him by Buraq to Jerusalem and the heavens.
rows.anchor: عن سليمان بن بلال، عن شريك بن أبي نمر، قال: سمعت أنسا، يحدثنا عن ليلة المسرى برسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من مسجد الكعبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the continuation of Anas's report, Moses advises seeking relief from fifty prayers until five remain, each counted as ten; the Prophet is embarrassed to ask again.
rows.anchor: ثم هبط حتى بلغ موسى فاحتبسه، فقال: يا محمد ماذا عهد إليك ربك؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says the soundest reading of “the Sacred Mosque” is the sanctuary commonly meant by the name; al-Aqṣā is Jerusalem, called farthest as the most distant visited mosque and second in merit.
rows.anchor: وأولى الأقوال في ذلك بالصواب، أن يقال: إن الله عز وجل أخبر أنه أسرى بعبده من المسجد الحرام

rows.speaker: بعض أهل العلم
rows.claim: One view holds that the Prophet's body physically traveled on Buraq from Mecca to Jerusalem, prayed with the prophets, ascended beyond seven heavens, and returned before dawn.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم: أسرى الله بجسده، فسار به ليلا على البراق من بيته الحرام إلى بيته الأقصى

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report through Ibn Shihāb, al-Musayyib, and Abū Salama describes the physical journey on Buraq to Jerusalem, where the Prophet chooses milk over wine and meets Abraham and Jesus.
rows.anchor: عن ابن شهاب، قال: أخبرني ابن المسيب، وأبو سلمة بن عبد الرحمن أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أسري به على البراق

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الصديق
rows.claim: When told the Prophet claimed to have traveled to Jerusalem and back in one night, Abū Bakr says he believes him as he believes news from heaven.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر: أوقال ذلك؟ قالوا: نعم، قال: فأشهد إن كان قال ذلك لقد صدق

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Jābir reports that when Quraysh denied him, God displayed Jerusalem before the Prophet so he could describe its landmarks while looking at it.
rows.anchor: سمعت جابر بن عبد الله يقول: سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas reports Gabriel admonished Buraq; the Prophet passed an old woman and tempting caller, then greeted Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, figures Gabriel identifies as worldly life, Satan, and prophets.
rows.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك، قال: لما جاء جبرائيل عليه السلام بالبراق إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: In Anas's account, the Prophet chooses milk; Gabriel calls it the natural way, saying water would drown the community while wine would lead them astray.
rows.anchor: فتناول رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم اللبن، فقال له جبرائيل: أصبت يا محمد الفطرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī corrects nāʾin for an old woman to feminine nāʾiya, noting that the feminine ending was omitted.
rows.anchor: قال أبو جعفر: ينبغي أن يقال: نائية، ولكن أسقط منها التأنيث

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة أو غيره عن النبي
rows.claim: A report whose attribution to Abū Hurayra the transmitter doubts describes Gabriel washing the Prophet's chest with Zamzam and filling it with faith, knowledge, certainty, and Islam.
rows.anchor: عن أبي العالية الرياحي، عن أبي هريرة، أو غيره شك أبو جعفر

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة أو غيره عن النبي
rows.claim: The fields of grain represent people striving in God's path: their reward multiplies seven hundredfold and God replaces what they spend.
rows.anchor: هؤلاء المجاهدون في سبيل الله، تضاعف لهم الحسنة بسبع مائة ضعف

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة أو غيره عن النبي
rows.claim: People whose heads are repeatedly crushed and restored represent those burdened by obligatory prayer.
rows.anchor: هؤلاء الذين تتثاقل رءوسهم عن الصلاة المكتوبة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة أو غيره عن النبي
rows.claim: People grazing and eating infernal food represent those who fail to pay required alms from their wealth.
rows.anchor: هؤلاء الذين لا يؤدون صدقات أموالهم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة أو غيره عن النبي
rows.claim: Those choosing foul raw meat over good cooked meat represent adulterous people abandoning lawful spouses for illicit partners.
rows.anchor: هذا الرجل من أمتك، تكون عنده المرأة الحلال الطيب، فيأتي امرأة خبيثة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة أو غيره عن النبي
rows.claim: A barrier tearing everything that passes represents people who block roads; the report quotes 7:86.
rows.anchor: ثم قرأ: {ولا تقعدوا بكل صراط توعدون وتصدون} [الأعراف: 86] الآية

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة أو غيره عن النبي
rows.claim: A man adding firewood he cannot carry represents someone burdened with people's deposits who cannot repay them but takes on more.
rows.anchor: هذا الرجل من أمتك تكون عنده أمانات الناس لا يقدر على أدائها، وهو يزيد عليها

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة أو غيره عن النبي
rows.claim: Preachers whose tongues and lips are repeatedly cut represent speakers of religious discord who say what they do not practice.
rows.anchor: هؤلاء خطباء أمتك خطباء الفتنة يقولون ما لا يفعلون

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة أو غيره عن النبي
rows.claim: A huge bull unable to return through a tiny hole represents a person who says a grave word and cannot retract it.
rows.anchor: هذا الرجل يتكلم بالكلمة العظيمة، ثم يندم عليها، فلا يستطيع أن يردها

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة أو غيره عن النبي
rows.claim: Paradise asks God to fulfill its promise of delights; God promises it to believers who worship Him alone, do good, fear Him, and rely on Him.
rows.anchor: هذا صوت الجنة تقول: يا رب آتني ما وعدتني

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة أو غيره عن النبي
rows.claim: Hell asks God to fulfill its promise of torment; it is promised to associators, disbelievers, and tyrants who reject the Reckoning.
rows.anchor: هذا صوت جهنم، تقول: يا رب آتني ما وعدتني

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة أو غيره عن النبي
rows.claim: At Jerusalem the Prophet ties his mount at a rock and prays with the angels, who welcome him as brother and successor.
rows.anchor: ثم سار حتى أتى بيت المقدس، فنزل فربط فرسه إلى صخرة، ثم دخل فصلى مع الملائكة

rows.speaker: داود
rows.claim: David praises God for sovereignty, teaching him the Psalms, and softening iron.
rows.anchor: الحمد لله الذي جعل لي ملكا عظيما وعلمني الزبور، وألان لي الحديد

rows.speaker: سليمان
rows.claim: Solomon praises God for subjecting winds and demons to serve him and teaching him birds' speech.
rows.anchor: ثم إن سليمان أثنى على ربه، فقال: الحمد لله الذي سخر لي الرياح، وسخر لي الشياطين

rows.speaker: داود
rows.claim: David adds that God made mountains and birds praise with him and gave him wisdom and decisive speech.
rows.anchor: وسخر لي الجبال يسبحن والطير، وأعطاني الحكمة وفصل الخطاب

rows.speaker: سليمان
rows.claim: Solomon says God gave him unrivaled sovereignty and a gracious kingdom for which he has no reckoning.
rows.anchor: وآتاني ملكا عظيما لا ينبغي لأحد من بعدي، وجعل ملكي ملكا طيبا ليس علي فيه حساب

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: Jesus praises God for making him His word, teaching him scripture, granting miracles by God's permission, and protecting him and his mother from Satan.
rows.anchor: الحمد لله الذي جعلني كلمته وجعل مثلي مثل آدم خلقه من تراب

rows.speaker: محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Muhammad praises God for sending him as mercy and universal bearer of good news and warning, revealing the Furqān, and making his community best, middle, first, and last.
rows.anchor: الحمد لله الذي أرسلني رحمة للعالمين، وكافة للناس بشيرا ونذيرا، وأنزل علي الفرقان

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر الرازي
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar al-Rāzī explains Muhammad's being “seal and opener” as seal of prophecy and opener of intercession on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: قال أبو جعفر وهو الرازي: خاتم النبوة، وفاتح بالشفاعة يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet chooses milk among three vessels; Gabriel says wine will be forbidden to the community and choosing it would leave only a few followers.
rows.anchor: فقال: «لا أريده قد رويت» فقال له جبرائيل صلى الله عليه وسلم: أما إنها ستحرم على أمتك

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The ascent account identifies Adam by the gates of Paradise and Hell, Jesus and John as maternal cousins, Joseph as exceptionally handsome, then Idrīs, Aaron, and Moses; Moses weeps when Muhammad passes him.
rows.anchor: قال: هذا أبوك آدم، وهذا الباب الذي عن يمينه باب الجنة

rows.speaker: موسى
rows.claim: Moses says he weeps because Israel claimed he was most honored by God, while Muhammad has succeeded him in earthly life and has a community with him.
rows.anchor: قال: موسى، قال: «فما باله يبكي؟» قال: تزعم بنو إسرائيل

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن جبرائيل
rows.claim: At the seventh heaven, Abraham is identified as the Prophet's father; the white-faced did not mingle faith with wrongdoing, while the mixed-complexioned are repentant sinners purified by three rivers.
rows.anchor: وأما هؤلاء الذين في ألوانهم شيء، فقوم خلطوا عملا صالحا وآخر سيئا، فتابوا، فتاب الله عليهم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن جبرائيل
rows.claim: The Sidrat al-Muntahā is the endpoint for members of the Prophet's community who follow his practice, and bears rivers of pure water, milk, wine, and honey.
rows.anchor: هذه السدرة ينتهي إليها كل أحد خلا من أمتك على سنتك

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: At the Lote Tree, God speaks to the Prophet and recounts distinctive favors given to Abraham, Moses, David, Solomon, and Jesus.
rows.anchor: فكلمه عند ذلك، فقال له: سل، فقال: «اتخذت إبراهيم خليلا وأعطيته ملكا عظيما

rows.speaker: الله تعالى
rows.claim: God's address gives Muhammad universal mission, expanded breast and renown, a middle community that is first and last, the seven oft-repeated verses, al-Kawthar, and eight obligations; he was first created among prophets and last sent.
rows.anchor: فقال له ربه: قد اتخذتك حبيبا وخليلا، وهو مكتوب في التوراة: حبيب الله

rows.speaker: محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Muhammad lists six distinctions: opening and closing expressions, comprehensive speech, mission to all, fear cast into enemies from a month's distance, lawful spoils, and the earth as purification and prayer.
rows.anchor: فقال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: " فضلني ربي بست: أعطاني فواتح الكلم وخواتيمه

rows.speaker: محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Moses repeatedly advises Muhammad to request relief from fifty prayers; the obligation falls by tens and then five, which counts as fifty, and Muhammad declines to ask again out of modesty.
rows.anchor: وفرض علي خمسين صلاة "، فلما رجع إلى موسى، قال: بم أمرت يا محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narration says Moses was most insistent in advising Muhammad on the first pass and kindest when he returned.
rows.anchor: فكان موسى أشدهم عليه حين مر به، وخيرهم له حين رجع إليه

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة عن أبي العالية
rows.claim: A parallel report through Abū al-ʿĀliya, with uncertainty in the chain, mostly matches the earlier night-journey account but varies details of the punished groups and Lote Tree.
rows.anchor: عن أبي العالية أو غيره شك أبو جعفر عن أبي هريرة في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī notes this parallel account adds Michael with Gabriel and varies other details from Ali ibn Sahl's version.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه، قال: جاء جبرائيل ومعه ميكائيل

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd reports the Prophet describing Buraq as a mount previously ridden by prophets; he passes calls from Judaism, Christianity, and worldly life, chooses milk, then receives a ladder for ascending souls.
rows.anchor: فقال نبي الله: " أتيت بدابة هي أشبه الدواب بالبغل
